newsitem.title: USA: US bank reform adds broker exams for bank workers.
newsitem.headline: US bank reform adds broker exams for bank workers.

text.p: The House Banking Committee voted on Thursday to amend financial sector reform legislation to require bank employees who sell securities to pass the same exams required of securities firm employees.

On an 18 to 14 vote, the panel approved an amendment by Texas Democrat Ken Bentsen requiring banks that sell securities to join the National Association of Securities Dealers, a private organization that oversees some securities regulation under the auspices of the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Under current law, banks that deal in a limited range of securities including Treasury bonds and municipal general obligation bonds are not regulated by the NASD or the SEC.
Bank subsidiaries that deal in other so-called ineligible securities, such as equities and corporate bonds, are subject to SEC oversight.
"It's not a very large group, but still an important group that does have contact with the public," Rep. Bentsen said.
Committee chairman Jim Leach, Republican of Iowa, opposed the amendment, calling it "unnecessary" and "over-broad."
Federal bank regulators have proposed requiring bank employees who sell securities to take the NASD exams, but not requiring banks to join the self-regulatory organization.
Banking groups opposed the amendment, which they said would subject banks to NASD regulation, requiring record keeping and auditing, even for ordinary banking activities.
"It's a big problem," Sally Miller, lobbyist for the American Bankers Association, told reporters after the vote.

Miller said the language of the amendment would encompass banks actively managing their own investment portfolios, managing fiduciary accounts, offering sweep accounts involving mutual funds and private placement activity.
